record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own model-size and training-time results for test performance, using MNIST MLP sweeps rather than a direct measurement designed to identify double descent.
record.gate_note: The study reports that test accuracy typically rises with network size among models that fit the training data, and describes test accuracy over training time as rising to a maximum before declining slightly. It does not report a measured interpolation-threshold peak. Results about gradient regularization, parameter perturbations, and explicit regularization do not directly test the claim versions. Double-descent statements in cited work are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: This is a study of implicit gradient regularization. It cites Belkin et al. 2019 only as background. Its size sweep keeps only MNIST MLPs that reach 100% training accuracy and scores each at its maximum test accuracy, which amounts to early stopping. So the region near the interpolation threshold and any test-error peak are never measured. Its training-time curves run up to 250k iterations on clean MNIST and were not designed to look for a second descent. No result bears on whether any double-descent version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that discrete gradient-descent steps implicitly penalize the squared loss-gradient norm, with strength proportional to learning rate and network size. They say this biases training toward flatter minima with higher test accuracy and robustness to parameter noise, and that the same term works as an explicit regularizer (ResNet-18 test accuracy up by more than 12%). They make no double-descent claim.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates gradient-descent regularization and its relationship to test performance; it does not implement or measure the original sources' double-descent procedure or interpolation-threshold curve.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported comparisons vary network size and learning rate. The authors also note that comparisons depend on stopping-time choice, and report alternative stopping-time analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Among MNIST MLPs that fit the training set, scored at maximum test accuracy, test accuracy typically rises with network size and learning rate, and is strongly correlated with lower R_IG (Figure A.6, Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit gradient regularization strength (proportional to learning rate × parameter count) predicts test accuracy of interpolating networks.

record.problems: The size result is described as a typical trend among models selected to fit the training data, without a reported pre-threshold segment or peak location. The temporal result is described qualitatively, with no exact values or uncertainty reported for these claim-relevant comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported result was omitted. Gradient-regularization values, parameter-noise robustness, and explicit-gradient-regularization results were not entered because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: no sweep through the interpolation threshold and no test error measured without early stopping.
All of it: no long-training or label-noise setup in which a second descent could appear.
No effective-complexity measure used to predict where the peak falls.
No label-noise manipulation and no tuned-regularization study of a peak. Explicit gradient regularization is studied only for test-accuracy gains.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's verdicts ('supports' V1, 'challenges' V2) should be dropped. Early stopping at maximum test accuracy is known to suppress the double-descent peak, so neither row can speak to V1 or V2.

versions.untested_parts: The study considers only models selected to reach 100% training accuracy for its size comparisons; it does not report the pre-interpolation decline or locate a peak near the size that first fits the training set.
The training-time results are reported by iteration, not as a separate epoch-wise analysis, and do not locate a peak in relation to the training-set interpolation point.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold is reported.
No double-descent comparison across model classes is reported.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study does not test whether label noise or variance drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
The study does not re-count complexity by an effective number of parameters or test whether that yields an ordinary U-shaped curve.

conditions.value: 100%; models that failed to reach this were excluded

rows.measure: Test accuracy as network size increases
rows.value: Test accuracy typically increases as network size increases; exact per-size values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The text describes a typical trend over the selected, training-set-fitting networks; Figure A.6 plots the size comparisons. This is evidence for the post-fit improvement direction only, not for the full fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: Only networks that fit the training set are kept, each scored at its maximum-test-accuracy iteration. This early-stopped, post-interpolation selection cannot show the first descent or the threshold peak. Also, size and learning rate are mixed together in Figure A.6, and per-size values are only plotted. 'Observed' overstates what the row shows.

rows.subject: MLPs trained on MNIST (aggregate across plotted learning rates)
rows.operation_detail: Measured test accuracy over training iterations.
rows.value: Test accuracy increases during training until reaching a maximum, then decreases slightly; exact values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The reported temporal pattern lacks the fall-rise-fall shape; the text characterizes the post-maximum decline as slight. The figure shows the curves, but the text does not give exact values.
rows.check: Figure A.4 shows test accuracy rising, then declining slightly (test loss falls, then rises) over 250k iterations on clean-label MNIST. A missing second descent within a finite window, with no label noise and no design aimed at epoch-wise double descent, cannot show the effect is absent. 'Absent' and the 'challenges' verdict are not justified.
